newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albania govt faces uphill task to restore order.
newsitem.headline: Albania govt faces uphill task to restore order.

text.p: Albania's new government on Tuesday sought parliamentary support for its policies to restore law and order as mafia gangs battled in the town of Vlore following the pullout of foreign troops.

Newly-appointed ministers in the Socialist-led government outlined plans before parliament ahead of a confidence vote due later on Tuesday which the new five-party coalition was expected to win easily.

Interior Minister Neritan Ceka said police would first try to wrest back highways from gangsters who have robbed travellers for months, then move to crack down on criminals using some southern towns as personal fiefdoms.

But the government faces an uphill task to restore peace, particularly in the south and the Adriatic port town of Vlore, where protests over failed investment schemes in February spiraled into widespread anarchy.

The withdrawal from Vlore of Italian and Greek troops, sent to Albania in March as part of a multinational security force, has left the town at the mercy of gangs which, according to some residents, appeared to be fighting each other continually.
"Until the Italians were here two days ago, the gangs fought each other in the night but now the Italians have left, they are fighting in broad daylight," one Vlore resident said.

Police chief Haxhi Demiri said the situation had deteriorated and he was concerned that the government was dragging its feet and failing to take rapid action to help combat what he described as "organised armies".

Ceka said police were badly in need of bullet-proof vests and other equipment that would be some of the main priorities raised at initial talks in Rome on Wednesday ahead of an aid conference scheduled for October.
"A police chief died in a clash with bandits although we sent him to Greece (for treatment). He could have lived if he had had a bullet-proof vest," Ceka said.

Nine people were killed in gangland crime or revenge attacks in the last 24 hours, the interior ministry said. Around a million guns, looted from armouries, are in private hands or in the possession of gangs.
More than 1,500 people have been killed in the poverty-stricken, former communist country in the Balkans since unrest erupted following the collapse of pyramid investment schemes five months ago.
The violence brought down the Democratic Party government and led to early elections in June in which the Democrats lost out heavily to the Socialists.
The result also led to the downfall of president Sali Berisha, who resigned last week.
Ceka also gave warning of possible further trouble from elements within the SHIK secret service loyal to Berisha and his administration.
He said they may try to stir unrest in northern Albania and that police could not rely on the secret service for information because its intelligence network had disintegrated.

Addressing parliament for the first time on Monday, Prime Minister Fatos Nano painted a bleak economic picture. He pledged a campaign to halt a further erosion of gross domestic product as well as soaring inflation, expected to reach up to 50 percent by the end of 1997.
